## Solution

Let $S: x^2+y^2+z^2=R^2$ with outward normal. We compute
$$I=\iint_S \frac{dx\,dy}{z}+\frac{dy\,dz}{x}+\frac{dx\,dz}{y}=I_1+I_2+I_3$$
by projecting onto the coordinate planes.

### Term $I_1=\iint_S \frac{dx\,dy}{z}$

Project onto the $xy$-plane; the projection is the disk $D:\ x^2+y^2\le R^2$. Split $S$ into the upper hemisphere ($z=+\sqrt{R^2-x^2-y^2}$, outward normal $n_z>0$, sign $+$) and lower hemisphere ($z=-\sqrt{R^2-x^2-y^2}$, $n_z<0$, sign $-$):

$$I_1=\iint_D \frac{dx\,dy}{\sqrt{R^2-x^2-y^2}}+\iint_D \frac{(-1)\,dx\,dy}{-\sqrt{R^2-x^2-y^2}}=2\iint_D\frac{dx\,dy}{\sqrt{R^2-x^2-y^2}}.$$

Polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$:
$$I_1=2\int_0^{2\pi}d\theta\int_0^R\frac{r\,dr}{\sqrt{R^2-r^2}}=4\pi\Big[-\sqrt{R^2-r^2}\Big]_0^R=4\pi R.$$

### Term $I_2=\iint_S \frac{dy\,dz}{x}$

By the identical argument, project onto the $yz$-plane (disk $y^2+z^2\le R^2$), split into $x>0$ ($n_x>0$, sign $+$) and $x<0$ ($n_x<0$, sign $-$):

$$I_2=2\iint_{y^2+z^2\le R^2}\frac{dy\,dz}{\sqrt{R^2-y^2-z^2}}=4\pi R.$$

### Term $I_3=\iint_S \frac{dx\,dz}{y}$

Project onto the $xz$-plane (disk $D'':\ x^2+z^2\le R^2$). Split into the front hemisphere ($y=+\sqrt{R^2-x^2-z^2}$, $n_y>0$, sign $+$) and back hemisphere ($y=-\sqrt{R^2-x^2-z^2}$, $n_y<0$, sign $-$):

$$I_3=\iint_{D''}\frac{dx\,dz}{\sqrt{R^2-x^2-z^2}}+\iint_{D''}\frac{(-1)\,dx\,dz}{-\sqrt{R^2-x^2-z^2}}=2\iint_{D''}\frac{dx\,dz}{\sqrt{R^2-x^2-z^2}}.$$

Polar coordinates on the $xz$-plane:
$$I_3=2\int_0^{2\pi}d\theta\int_0^R\frac{r\,dr}{\sqrt{R^2-r^2}}=4\pi R.$$

### Total

$$\boxed{I=I_1+I_2+I_3=4\pi R+4\pi R+4\pi R=12\pi R.}$$

**Remark on why Gauss–Ostrogradsky fails.** Writing the integrand as $P\,dy\,dz+Q\,dz\,dx+R\,dx\,dy$ with $P=1/x,\ Q=1/y,\ R=1/z$, the divergence is $\operatorname{div}=-1/x^2-1/y^2-1/z^2$, which is singular at the origin. The volume integral $\iiint_B(-1/x^2-1/y^2-1/z^2)\,dV$ diverges, so the divergence theorem cannot be applied—exactly why the problem requires direct computation.
